# Free-Form Geometry: B-Splines {#sec-bsplines}

::: {.chapter-abstract}
The one non-analytic shape STEP needs, because every CAD kernel converges on it.
What the eight parameters after the name in a B-spline record are, why a circle written as a spline has seven control points and weights of one-half, and how to tell a real free-form surface from an analytic one in disguise.
:::

A plane, a cylinder and a sphere can each be written down with a handful of numbers because each is a closed-form equation.
A car body panel, a turbine blade or a filleted corner blended between three faces cannot.
Every CAD system represents those as **B-spline** curves and surfaces — specifically, non-uniform rational B-splines, **NURBS** — and so does STEP.
It is the only free-form representation in Part 42 that matters, and it can also represent every analytic shape exactly, which is why exporters sometimes write circles and cylinders as splines.

::: {.callout-note title="Engineering background: NURBS in one page"}
A B-spline curve is a smooth path controlled by a sequence of **control points**.
It does not, in general, pass through them; it is pulled toward them, the way a flexible ruler is bent by pegs.
Three things fix its shape:

**Degree.** The polynomial degree of the pieces.
Degree 1 gives straight segments between control points; degree 2 gives parabolic arcs; degree 3, cubic, is the usual choice for free-form work because it is the lowest degree that can be smooth in curvature.
The number of polynomial pieces is the number of distinct knot intervals inside the curve's parameter range.
For a clamped curve whose interior knots are all distinct, a degree-$p$ curve with $n$ control points has $n - p$ of them; repeated interior knots reduce the count.

**Knots.** A non-decreasing list of parameter values that says where one piece ends and the next begins.
The knot vector has $n + p + 1$ entries.
Repeating a knot value $p$ times forces the curve *through* a control point (and lets it have a corner there); repeating the first and last knots $p + 1$ times **clamps** the curve so that it starts and ends exactly at the first and last control points.
Almost every curve in a CAD file is clamped.
Knots that are evenly spaced give a *uniform* B-spline; STEP's are *non-uniform* in general.

**Weights.** A **rational** B-spline attaches a positive weight to each control point; a heavier point pulls harder.
Weights are what let a spline represent a circle *exactly*, which a polynomial spline cannot.
A curve whose weights are all 1 is *non-rational*, and the weights are omitted.

A B-spline **surface** is the same construction in two parameters, $u$ and $v$: a rectangular *grid* of control points, a degree in each direction, a knot vector in each direction, and optionally a grid of weights.
Every point on the surface is a weighted blend of a $(p + 1) \times (q + 1)$ window of control points.

None of this is needed to *read* a STEP file — the records are just lists of numbers — but it is needed to know which list is which, and to recognise the special cases.
:::

## A B-spline curve record {#sec-bsplines-curve-record}

From the cone of @sec-curves-surfaces, its straight seam written as a spline:

```step
#33 = B_SPLINE_CURVE_WITH_KNOTS('',1,(#34,#35),.UNSPECIFIED.,.F.,.F.,
        (2,2),(0.,1.),.PIECEWISE_BEZIER_KNOTS.);
#34 = CARTESIAN_POINT('',(5.,0.,0.));
#35 = CARTESIAN_POINT('',(2.,0.,10.));
```

The attributes, from the inheritance chain `representation_item` → `b_spline_curve` → `b_spline_curve_with_knots`:

| Parameter | Attribute | Declared in |
|---|---|---|
| `''` | `name` | `representation_item` |
| `1` | `degree` | `b_spline_curve` |
| `(#34,#35)` | `control_points_list` | `b_spline_curve` |
| `.UNSPECIFIED.` | `curve_form` | `b_spline_curve` |
| `.F.` | `closed_curve` | `b_spline_curve` |
| `.F.` | `self_intersect` | `b_spline_curve` |
| `(2,2)` | `knot_multiplicities` | `b_spline_curve_with_knots` |
| `(0.,1.)` | `knots` | `b_spline_curve_with_knots` |
| `.PIECEWISE_BEZIER_KNOTS.` | `knot_spec` | `b_spline_curve_with_knots` |

Degree 1, two control points: a straight segment from (5, 0, 0) to (2, 0, 10).
The knots are stored compressed — *distinct values* with *multiplicities* rather than the full vector — so `(2,2)` and `(0.,1.)` expand to the knot vector (0, 0, 1, 1): $n + p + 1 = 2 + 1 + 1 = 4$ entries, with the ends repeated $p + 1 = 2$ times.
Clamped, as promised.

`curve_form` is a hint: `.POLYLINE_FORM.`, `.CIRCULAR_ARC.`, `.ELLIPTIC_ARC.`, `.PARABOLIC_ARC.`, `.HYPERBOLIC_ARC.` or `.UNSPECIFIED.`.
Writers almost always put `.UNSPECIFIED.` even when the curve is a circle, so the hint is rarely useful.
`closed_curve` and `self_intersect` are `LOGICAL` — `.T.`, `.F.` or `.U.` for unknown — and are what they say.
`knot_spec` describes the knot pattern: `.UNIFORM_KNOTS.`, `.QUASI_UNIFORM_KNOTS.`, `.PIECEWISE_BEZIER_KNOTS.` (every interior knot has multiplicity $p$, so each piece is an independent Bézier segment) or `.UNSPECIFIED.`.
It, too, is a hint; the multiplicities are the truth.

## A B-spline surface record {#sec-bsplines-surface-record}

From a small part whose top edge is a free-form spline extruded downward:

```step
#56 = B_SPLINE_SURFACE_WITH_KNOTS('',3,1,
        ((#57,#58),(#59,#60),(#61,#62),(#63,#64),(#65,#66),(#67,#68)),
        .UNSPECIFIED.,.F.,.F.,.F.,
        (4,1,1,4),(2,2),
        (0.,10.770329614269,22.43223340396,33.612573291459),(-5.,0.),
        .UNSPECIFIED.);
#57 = CARTESIAN_POINT('',(0.,0.,5.));
#58 = CARTESIAN_POINT('',(0.,0.,0.));
#59 = CARTESIAN_POINT('',(3.579071051472,4.965892889794,5.));
#60 = CARTESIAN_POINT('',(3.579071051472,4.965892889794,0.));
    /* ... three more pairs ... */
#67 = CARTESIAN_POINT('',(30.,3.,5.));
#68 = CARTESIAN_POINT('',(30.,3.,0.));
```

| Parameter | Attribute | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `3, 1` | `u_degree`, `v_degree` | cubic along *u*, linear along *v* |
| `((#57,#58),...,(#67,#68))` | `control_points_list` | a list of 6 rows, each of 2 points: a 6 × 2 grid |
| `.UNSPECIFIED.` | `surface_form` | hint (`.PLANE_SURF.`, `.CYLINDRICAL_SURF.`, …, `.UNSPECIFIED.`) |
| `.F., .F., .F.` | `u_closed`, `v_closed`, `self_intersect` | logicals |
| `(4,1,1,4), (2,2)` | `u_multiplicities`, `v_multiplicities` | |
| `(0.,10.77,22.43,33.61), (-5.,0.)` | `u_knots`, `v_knots` | distinct knot values |
| `.UNSPECIFIED.` | `knot_spec` | |

Read it as two curves at right angles.
Along *u*: degree 3, six control points, knots expanding to (0, 0, 0, 0, 10.77, 22.43, 33.61, 33.61, 33.61, 33.61) — ten entries, $6 + 3 + 1$, clamped at both ends, with two interior knots dividing the curve into three cubic pieces.
The interior knot values are the cumulative chord lengths of the points the original spline was fitted through, which is how the exporter's kernel parametrised it.
A reader never has to know that; the knots only have to be non-decreasing.
Along *v*: degree 1, two control points, knots (−5, −5, 0, 0).
A straight line.

Each row of the control grid is a pair of points with the same x and y and z = 5 or z = 0.
The surface is the *u*-curve — the free-form spline along the top of the part — swept straight down five millimetres.
It is, in other words, a `SURFACE_OF_LINEAR_EXTRUSION`, and the exporter that wrote this file was asked to convert everything to NURBS, so it wrote it as one.
Nothing in the record says "extrusion"; you can only tell from the degree-1 *v* direction and the parallel rows.

## Rational splines: the circle as a spline {#sec-bsplines-rational}

Convert the pin of @sec-curves-surfaces to NURBS and its circles come out like this:

```step
#31 = ( BOUNDED_CURVE()
        B_SPLINE_CURVE(2,(#32,#33,#34,#35,#36,#37,#38),.UNSPECIFIED.,.T.,.F.)
        B_SPLINE_CURVE_WITH_KNOTS((1,2,2,2,2,1),
          (-2.094395102393,0.,2.094395102393,4.188790204786,6.28318530718,8.377580409573),
          .UNSPECIFIED.)
        CURVE()
        GEOMETRIC_REPRESENTATION_ITEM()
        RATIONAL_B_SPLINE_CURVE((1.,0.5,1.,0.5,1.,0.5,1.))
        REPRESENTATION_ITEM('') );
```

A complex instance, and @sec-schema says why: `RATIONAL_B_SPLINE_CURVE` and `B_SPLINE_CURVE_WITH_KNOTS` are *sibling* subtypes of `b_spline_curve` — one adds weights, the other adds knots — and a curve that needs both has no single leaf name.
So the record is written externally: every type in the chain, alphabetically, each with its own attributes.
`BOUNDED_CURVE`, `CURVE`, `GEOMETRIC_REPRESENTATION_ITEM` and `REPRESENTATION_ITEM` are the supertypes contributing nothing but the name.

The content is the textbook NURBS circle.
Degree 2.
Seven control points.
Weights alternating 1, ½, 1, ½, 1, ½, 1.
Knots expanding to (−2.094, 0, 0, 2.094, 2.094, 4.189, 4.189, 6.283, 6.283, 8.378) — ten entries, $7 + 2 + 1$, with every interior knot doubled.
Three pieces, each a quadratic rational arc spanning 120° (2.094 radians), joined at the knots of multiplicity 2, meeting to form a full circle.
The half-weight points are the corners of the circumscribing triangle; the unit-weight points lie on the circle.
`closed_curve` is `.T.`.
The knot values are angles in radians because that is how the kernel parametrised the original circle.
This curve is *not* clamped: its end multiplicities are 1, not $p + 1$, and the outer knots at −2.094 and 8.378 lie outside the curve's actual range of 0 to 2π.
That is how a closed periodic curve is written, and it is the common exception to the rule that CAD curves are clamped.

The equivalent surface — the pin's cylindrical side as a rational B-spline — is the same construction in *u* with a degree-1 straight line in *v*, and its weights are a 7 × 2 grid.

## Recognising analytic geometry in spline clothing {#sec-bsplines-recognising}

A file can legitimately contain a cylinder written as `CYLINDRICAL_SURFACE` or as a rational B-spline surface, and a reader may need to know that they are the same shape.
Some exporters convert everything to NURBS on the way out (older CATIA translators did this for anything not planar).
The signs:

- A degree-1 curve with two control points is a **line**.
- A degree-2 rational curve with 7 control points, weights (1, ½)\*, and knots of multiplicity 2 at 120° intervals is a **full circle**. Quarter-circles use 3 control points and weights (1, $\sqrt{2}/2$, 1). Other arc splits exist.
- A surface with degree 1 in one direction and control rows that are translates of each other is an **extrusion**.
- A surface with degree 2 rational in one direction with the circle pattern, and degree 1 in the other, is a **cylinder**.
- A surface whose control net is planar is a **plane** (a bilinear 2 × 2 patch, as `#92` in the same file: degree 1 in both directions, four points).

None of this is required.
Any reader that can evaluate a NURBS can evaluate these.
But a tool that wants to report "this part has 14 cylindrical holes," or to compare two files for equivalence, has to look through the representation to the shape.

## What the geometry chapters leave out {#sec-bsplines-leave-out}

Part 42 defines several more B-spline forms — `BEZIER_CURVE`, `QUASI_UNIFORM_CURVE`, `UNIFORM_CURVE` and their surface equivalents — which are B-splines with knot vectors implied by the name instead of stored.
They appear rarely; `..._WITH_KNOTS` is what every mainstream exporter writes.
It also defines `OFFSET_CURVE_3D`, `OFFSET_SURFACE`, `CURVE_REPLICA` and `SURFACE_REPLICA`, `RECTANGULAR_TRIMMED_SURFACE` (a surface cut to a parameter rectangle), and `CURVE_BOUNDED_SURFACE` (a surface cut by curves rather than by topology).
Each is what its name suggests, each is in the AP242 schema, and a reader that has understood the records in this chapter can look any of them up.

::: {.callout-important title="In brief"}
A B-spline record is degree, control points, three flags, and a knot vector stored as distinct values plus multiplicities; the full vector has $n + p + 1$ entries and is almost always clamped.
A surface is the same in two directions with a grid of control points.
Rational splines add a weight per control point and are written as complex instances because the rational and with-knots subtypes are siblings.
Circles are seven points with weights 1, ½ alternating; lines are degree 1 with two points; extrusions are degree 1 in one direction.
:::
